title: Micah 1:10–16
context: Micah continues his lament with a series of Judean towns, many apparently chosen for wordplay on their names. The WEB explains Beth Ophrah as meaning “House of Dust,” where the prophet rolls in the dust (1:10). Other suggested wordplays, and the locations of some towns, are uncertain and are held with caution. The opening line echoes David’s lament in 2 Samuel 1:20. The list includes Lachish, Micah’s home district of Moresheth Gath, and Adullam, and ends with a call to mourn children gone into captivity (1:16). Many readers connect the list with an invasion of Judah’s lowland towns, though the precise occasion is not stated.

verses.text: Don’t tell it in Gath. Don’t weep at all. At Beth Ophrah I have rolled myself in the dust.
verses.arminianNotes: “Don’t tell it in Gath.” Micah echoes David’s lament in 2 Samuel 1:20. Arminian readers see the prophet beginning a lament built on wordplay with the names of towns.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the echo of 2 Samuel 1:20 and the wordplay on Beth Ophrah, “House of Dust,” where the prophet rolls in the dust. Readers in this tradition see grief expressed through the names of Judah’s towns.

verses.text: Pass on, inhabitant of Shaphir, in nakedness and shame. The inhabitant of Zaanan won’t come out. The wailing of Beth Ezel will take from you his protection.
verses.arminianNotes: “Pass on, inhabitant of Shaphir, in nakedness and shame.” Arminian readers see the lament continuing through towns whose names may carry ironic meanings, though those meanings are uncertain.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the lament moving from town to town. Many interpreters suggest wordplays on Shaphir, Zaanan, and Beth Ezel, and readers in this tradition hold those explanations with caution.

verses.text: For the inhabitant of Maroth waits anxiously for good, because evil has come down from the LORD to the gate of Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes: “For the inhabitant of Maroth waits anxiously for good, because evil has come down from the LORD to the gate of Jerusalem.” Arminian readers see hope for relief disappointed as judgment arrives.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see disaster attributed to the LORD as just judgment. On how God uses a hostile power against his people, readers may consult the existing Judges 9:23 box rather than a new discussion here.

verses.text: Harness the chariot to the swift steed, inhabitant of Lachish. She was the beginning of sin to the daughter of Zion; for the transgressions of Israel were found in you.
verses.arminianNotes: “Harness the chariot to the swift steed, inhabitant of Lachish. She was the beginning of sin to the daughter of Zion.” Arminian readers see Lachish singled out as a source of Judah’s sin.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Lachish named as the place where Israel’s transgressions were found. The text does not specify the sin, and readers in this tradition avoid speculating beyond what it says.

verses.text: Therefore you will give a parting gift to Moresheth Gath. The houses of Achzib will be a deceitful thing to the kings of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: “Therefore you will give a parting gift to Moresheth Gath.” Arminian readers see Micah’s own region among the towns lamented, so the prophet grieves for his home as well as for Jerusalem.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see judgment reaching Micah’s home district. Many interpreters see wordplay in Achzib, “deceitful thing,” and readers in this tradition hold such meanings with caution.

verses.text: I will yet bring a conqueror to you, inhabitants of Mareshah. The glory of Israel will come to Adullam.
verses.arminianNotes: “I will yet bring a conqueror to you, inhabitants of Mareshah. The glory of Israel will come to Adullam.” Arminian readers see the nation’s glory reduced to hiding, perhaps recalling David at Adullam.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a reversal: Israel’s glory retreats to Adullam, where David once took refuge (1 Samuel 22:1). Readers in this tradition hold the precise meaning of the line with care.

verses.text: Shave your heads, and cut off your hair for the children of your delight. Enlarge your baldness like the vulture, for they have gone into captivity from you!
verses.arminianNotes: “Shave your heads, and cut off your hair for the children of your delight.” Arminian readers see signs of mourning as Zion grieves for children taken into captivity.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a call to mourn the coming exile. Shared ground: the chapter ends in grief over real loss, and readers in both traditions commonly read it with compassion rather than detachment.
